subject: Chemistry
text: What type of deviation from Raoult's law is shown by a mixture of phenol and aniline? Give reason. What will happen to the boiling point of the solution on mixing phenol and aniline? (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: Phenol and aniline show negative deviation from Raoult's law. This is because phenol (-OH) and aniline (-NH2) form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds with each other, which are stronger than the A-A and B-B interactions in the pure liquids. This lowers the escaping tendency of molecules, so the vapour pressure of the mixture is lower than expected from Raoult's law. As a result, the boiling point of the solution increases (it is higher than the boiling points of the pure components).
keyPoints: Negative deviation from Raoult's law
Strong A-B hydrogen bonding between phenol -OH and aniline -NH2
Vapour pressure lower than ideal, so boiling point of mixture increases

subject: Chemistry
text: Why are haloarenes less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution reaction? Give two reasons. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: 1. Resonance effect: In haloarenes, the lone pair on halogen is delocalised into the aromatic ring, giving the C-X bond partial double-bond character. This makes the bond shorter and stronger, so it is harder to break. 2. Hybridisation/electronegativity: The carbon attached to the halogen is sp2 hybridised, which is more electronegative than sp3 carbon, holding the C-X electrons more tightly. Also, the nucleophile is repelled by the electron-rich benzene ring, and the possible SN2-type backside attack is hindered by the ring.
keyPoints: Resonance gives C-X partial double bond character (shorter, stronger bond)
sp2 carbon is more electronegative, holds bonding pair more tightly
Instability of possible phenyl cation / hindered backside attack by ring

text: Give a chemical test to show that [Co(NH3)5SO4]Cl and [Co(NH3)5Cl]SO4 are ionisation isomers. What is meant by the 'Chelate effect'? Give an example. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: Chemical test: Add AgNO3 solution to each complex. [Co(NH3)5SO4]Cl gives a white precipitate of AgCl (since Cl− is the free counter ion), while [Co(NH3)5Cl]SO4 gives no precipitate with AgNO3 (Cl is coordinated). Conversely, adding BaCl2 solution: [Co(NH3)5Cl]SO4 gives a white precipitate of BaSO4 (free SO4^2−), while [Co(NH3)5SO4]Cl gives no precipitate with BaCl2 (SO4 is coordinated). This confirms the two compounds are ionisation isomers. Chelate effect: When a polydentate (chelating) ligand binds to a metal ion through two or more donor atoms forming a ring, the resulting complex (chelate) is more stable than the analogous complex with monodentate ligands. Example: [Ni(en)3]2+ is more stable than [Ni(NH3)6]2+.
keyPoints: AgNO3 test distinguishes free Cl− vs coordinated Cl
BaCl2 test distinguishes free SO4^2− vs coordinated SO4
Chelate effect: ring formation by polydentate ligand increases complex stability (e.g. en vs NH3)

subject: Chemistry
text: Differentiate between the following: (i) Peptide linkage and Glycosidic linkage (ii) Essential amino acids and Non-essential amino acids (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (i) Peptide linkage is the amide (-CO-NH-) bond formed between the -COOH group of one amino acid and the -NH2 group of another amino acid with loss of water; it links amino acids to form proteins. Glycosidic linkage is the (acetal-type) C-O-C bond formed between two monosaccharide units with loss of water; it links sugars to form disaccharides/polysaccharides. (ii) Essential amino acids cannot be synthesised by the human body and must be obtained through diet, e.g. valine, leucine. Non-essential amino acids can be synthesised by the body itself, e.g. glycine, alanine.
keyPoints: Peptide linkage: -CO-NH- bond between amino acids (proteins)
Glycosidic linkage: C-O-C bond between monosaccharides (carbohydrates)
Essential = must come from diet; non-essential = synthesised by body

text: Following reaction takes place in one step: 2A + B → 2C. How will the rate of above reaction change if the volume of the reaction vessel is decreased to one third of its original volume? Will there be any change in the order of reaction with the reduced volume? (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: Since the reaction occurs in a single step, order = molecularity, so Rate = k[A]^2[B]. Reducing the volume to 1/3 triples all concentrations. New rate = k(3[A])^2(3[B]) = 27 × k[A]^2[B], i.e. the rate increases 27 times. The order of the reaction does not change; order is an experimentally determined property of the rate law and is independent of concentration/volume changes.
keyPoints: Rate law: Rate = k[A]^2[B] (single-step, order = molecularity)
Tripling concentrations increases rate by 3^3 = 27 times
Order of reaction remains unchanged (3rd order, unaffected by volume)

text: For the first order thermal decomposition reaction, C2H5Cl(g) → C2H4(g) + HCl(g), following data was obtained: at t=0 s, total pressure = 0.30 atm; at t=30 s, total pressure = 0.50 atm. Calculate rate constant. [Given: log 3 = 0.48] (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: Let initial pressure of C2H5Cl = P0 = 0.30 atm. At time t, if x is the pressure decrease of C2H5Cl, total pressure Pt = (P0 − x) + x + x = P0 + x, so x = Pt − P0 = 0.50 − 0.30 = 0.20 atm. Using k = (2.303/t) log[P0/(P0 − x)] = (2.303/30) log[0.30/(0.30−0.20)] = (2.303/30) log(0.30/0.10) = (2.303/30) log 3 = (2.303/30)(0.48) ≈ 3.68 × 10⁻² s⁻¹.
keyPoints: Pt = P0 + x for this stoichiometry, so x = Pt − P0 = 0.20 atm

text: (i) Why is the Equilibrium Constant (Kc) related to E°cell and not to Ecell? (ii) Two metals 'A' and 'B' have standard electrode potential values of −0.24 V and +0.80 V respectively. Which of these will liberate hydrogen gas from dil. H2SO4? (iii) Write the cell reaction which occurs in lead storage battery when it is in charging. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (i) At equilibrium, Ecell = 0 (no net driving force), so Ecell cannot be linked to K. The relation ΔG° = −RT ln K = −nFE°cell uses standard electrode potentials, so Kc is related to E°cell (a fixed constant), not to the variable, concentration-dependent Ecell. (ii) Metal A (E° = −0.24 V) has a lower (more negative) reduction potential than H+/H2 (0 V), so it is more easily oxidised and will liberate H2 gas from dilute H2SO4. Metal B (+0.80 V) will not, since it is less easily oxidised than hydrogen. (iii) On charging, the reactions of the lead storage battery are reversed: at cathode, PbSO4 + 2H2O → PbO2 + SO4²⁻ + 4H⁺ + 2e⁻; at anode, PbSO4 + 2e⁻ → Pb + SO4²⁻. Overall: 2PbSO4(s) + 2H2O(l) → Pb(s) + PbO2(s) + 2H2SO4(aq).
keyPoints: K relates to E° because Ecell = 0 at equilibrium
Metal A (−0.24 V, more negative than H+/H2) liberates H2; metal B does not
Charging reaction reverses discharge: 2PbSO4+2H2O → Pb+PbO2+2H2SO4

subject: Chemistry
text: What type of battery is Mercury cell? Why is it more advantageous than dry cell? Write overall reaction taking place in Mercury cell. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: Mercury cell is a primary battery (cannot be recharged/reused once the reactants are consumed). It is more advantageous than the dry cell because it gives a steady, constant voltage throughout its life, since the overall cell reaction does not involve any ion in solution whose concentration changes with time. Reactions: Anode: Zn(Hg) + 2OH⁻ → ZnO(s) + H2O + 2e⁻; Cathode: HgO(s) + H2O + 2e⁻ → Hg(l) + 2OH⁻. Overall: Zn(Hg) + HgO(s) → ZnO(s) + Hg(l).
keyPoints: Mercury cell is a primary (non-rechargeable) cell
Gives constant voltage since no ion concentration changes during use
Overall reaction: Zn(Hg) + HgO → ZnO + Hg

text: Calculate the boiling point of a solution containing 0.61 g of benzoic acid (Molar mass = 122 g mol⁻¹) in 5 g of CS2 in which it dimerises to the extent of 88%. The boiling point and Kb of CS2 are 46.2°C and 2.3 K kg mol⁻¹ respectively. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: Moles of benzoic acid = 0.61/122 = 0.005 mol. Molality m = 0.005 mol / 0.005 kg = 1 mol/kg. For dimerisation with degree of association α = 0.88, van't Hoff factor i = 1 − α + α/2 = 1 − 0.88 + 0.44 = 0.56. ΔTb = i × Kb × m = 0.56 × 2.3 × 1 = 1.288 K. Boiling point of solution = 46.2 + 1.288 ≈ 47.49°C.
keyPoints: i = 1 − α + α/2 for dimerisation, α=0.88 → i = 0.56
molality = 0.005 mol / 0.005 kg = 1 mol/kg
ΔTb = i·Kb·m ≈ 1.29 K; boiling point ≈ 47.5°C

subject: Chemistry
text: Write the reactions of D-Glucose with the following: (a) HI (b) Br2 water (c) Conc. HNO3 (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (a) With HI (strong reducing agent, prolonged reaction): all -OH groups and the -CHO group of glucose are reduced, and the product is n-hexane. (b) With bromine water (mild oxidising agent): only the -CHO group is oxidised to -COOH, giving gluconic acid (a monocarboxylic acid). (c) With concentrated HNO3 (strong oxidising agent): both the -CHO group and the terminal -CH2OH group are oxidised to -COOH, giving saccharic acid (glucaric acid, a dicarboxylic acid).
keyPoints: HI (excess/prolonged): reduces glucose completely to n-hexane
Br2 water: oxidises only -CHO to -COOH, giving gluconic acid
Conc. HNO3: oxidises both -CHO and -CH2OH to -COOH, giving saccharic acid

subject: Chemistry
text: Give reasons for the following: (a) Carboxylic acids have higher boiling point than alcohols of comparable molecular masses. (b) Alpha hydrogens of aldehydes and ketones are acidic in nature. (c) Nucleophilic addition of ammonia and its derivatives does not occur with carbonyl group in strongly acidic medium. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (a) Carboxylic acid molecules associate through two hydrogen bonds to form stable cyclic dimers, so more energy is required to break these stronger, more extensive H-bonds than the single H-bonds in alcohols, giving carboxylic acids higher boiling points. (b) Removal of an alpha-hydrogen gives a carbanion that is stabilised by resonance/delocalisation with the adjacent carbonyl group (forming an enolate-type structure), so alpha-hydrogens are relatively acidic. (c) In strongly acidic medium, ammonia/amine derivatives get protonated to form ammonium ions, which lose their lone pair and hence their nucleophilic character, so they cannot attack the carbonyl carbon.
keyPoints: Carboxylic acids form stronger cyclic dimers via two H-bonds than alcohols
Alpha-carbanion is resonance-stabilised by the carbonyl group (acidic alpha-H)
Strong acid protonates the amine, destroying its nucleophilicity

subject: Chemistry
text: Write the reaction involved in the following: (a) Reimer-Tiemann reaction (b) Kolbe's reaction (c) Friedal-Crafts acylation of anisole (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (a) Reimer-Tiemann reaction: Phenol reacts with CHCl3 and excess NaOH at 340 K; after hydrolysis, salicylaldehyde (o-hydroxybenzaldehyde) is formed as the major product. (b) Kolbe's reaction: Sodium phenoxide reacts with CO2 at 400 K and 4-7 atm pressure to give sodium salicylate, which on acidification gives salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid). (c) Friedel-Crafts acylation of anisole: Anisole reacts with CH3COCl in the presence of anhydrous AlCl3 to give a mixture of ortho- and para-methoxyacetophenone, with para as the major product (since -OCH3 is o,p-directing).
keyPoints: Reimer-Tiemann: phenol + CHCl3/NaOH → salicylaldehyde
Kolbe's reaction: sodium phenoxide + CO2 → salicylic acid
Friedel-Crafts acylation of anisole gives predominantly para-methoxyacetophenone

subject: Chemistry
text: Compound 'X' with molecular formula C4H9Br reacts with aqueous KOH to give an alcohol. The rate of this reaction depends only on the concentration of the compound 'X'. When an optically active isomer 'Y' of the compound 'X' was treated with aqueous KOH solution, the rate of reaction was found to be dependent on concentration of compound 'Y' and aqueous KOH both. (a) Write down the structural formula of both 'X' and 'Y'. (b) Out of 'X' and 'Y', which one will undergo racemisation and why? (c) Out of 'X' and 'Y', which one will form product with inversion of configuration and why? (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (a) X undergoes SN1 (rate depends only on [X]), so X is the tertiary bromide: (CH3)3C-Br (2-bromo-2-methylpropane). Y undergoes SN2 (rate depends on both [Y] and [KOH]) and is optically active, so Y is the chiral secondary bromide: CH3-CH2-CHBr-CH3 (2-bromobutane). (b) X (the SN1 substrate) will undergo racemisation, because the reaction proceeds via a planar, sp2 hybridised carbocation intermediate that can be attacked by OH⁻ from either face, giving a racemic mixture. (c) Y (the SN2 substrate) forms product with inversion of configuration (Walden inversion), because the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite to the leaving group in a single concerted step.
keyPoints: X = tert-butyl bromide (SN1); Y = 2-bromobutane (SN2, chiral)
X racemises via planar carbocation intermediate
Y shows inversion of configuration (backside attack, SN2)

subject: Chemistry
text: Case study: Amines react with mineral acids to form ammonium salts, showing basic character; aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia while aromatic amines are weaker. (a)(i) Why is CH3-NH2 a stronger base than (CH3)3N in aqueous solution? (ii) Identify A and B: CH3CONH2 --NaOBr--> A; A + C6H5COCl --> B. (b) A compound 'X' with molecular formula C3H9N reacts with Hinsberg reagent to give a product insoluble in alkali. Identify 'X'. (c) Why is -NH2 group of aniline acetylated before carrying out nitration? (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (a)(i) In aqueous solution, basicity depends on both the electron-donating (+I) effect of alkyl groups AND how well the resulting ammonium cation is solvated (stabilised) by water. In trimethylamine, the three bulky methyl groups cause steric hindrance that hinders solvation of the (CH3)3NH+ ion by water. In CH3NH2, there is much less steric crowding, so CH3NH3+ is solvated more effectively, making CH3NH2 the stronger base overall despite having fewer alkyl groups. (ii) CH3CONH2 undergoes the Hofmann bromamide degradation with NaOBr to give A = CH3NH2 (methanamine, one carbon less). A (CH3NH2) then reacts with C6H5COCl by nucleophilic acyl substitution to give B = C6H5CONHCH3 (N-methylbenzamide). (b) A product insoluble in alkali with Hinsberg's reagent indicates a secondary amine (the N,N-dialkyl sulfonamide formed has no acidic N-H left to dissolve in alkali). So X = CH3-NH-C2H5 (N-methylethanamine), a secondary amine with formula C3H9N. (c) The -NH2 group is a strong activator, and if aniline is nitrated directly, conc. HNO3 (being a strong oxidising agent) would oxidise the amine group, and the reaction would also give unwanted meta product due to protonation of NH2 to the meta-directing anilinium ion. Acetylation converts -NH2 to -NHCOCH3, which is still o,p-directing but less strongly activating and resistant to oxidation, giving a controlled, predominantly para-substituted product.
keyPoints: Steric hindrance to solvation makes (CH3)3N a weaker base than CH3NH2 in water
A = CH3NH2 (Hofmann bromamide degradation); B = C6H5CONHCH3
X = N-methylethanamine, CH3-NH-C2H5 (secondary amine, insoluble Hinsberg product)
Acetylation moderates activation and prevents oxidation/meta-substitution during nitration of aniline

subject: Chemistry
text: How can you convert aniline to benzonitrile? (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: Aniline is first converted to benzenediazonium chloride by treatment with NaNO2/HCl at 273-278 K (diazotisation). The diazonium salt is then treated with CuCN/KCN (Sandmeyer-type reaction) to replace the -N2+ group with -CN, giving benzonitrile (C6H5CN).
keyPoints: Aniline + NaNO2/HCl, 0-5°C → benzenediazonium chloride
Diazonium salt + CuCN/KCN → benzonitrile (Sandmeyer reaction)

subject: Chemistry
text: Case study: Valence Bond Theory (VBT) and Crystal Field Theory (CFT) explain the geometry, magnetic behaviour and d-orbital splitting in coordination compounds. (a) In octahedral crystal field, energies of which d-orbitals will be raised when ligands approach the central metal atom/ion? Give reason. (b) Using crystal field theory, write the electronic configuration of central metal ion of: (i) [CoF6]3− (ii) [Co(NH3)6]3+ [At. No. Co=27]. (c) [NiCl4]2− is paramagnetic while [Ni(CO)4] is diamagnetic though both are tetrahedral. Why? [At. No. Ni=28] (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (a) The eg set (dz2 and dx2−y2) is raised in energy, because these orbitals point directly along the axes towards the approaching ligands, experiencing greater electrostatic repulsion than the t2g orbitals, which point between the axes. (b) Co3+ is d6. (i) [CoF6]3−: F− is a weak field ligand, so it is high spin: t2g4 eg2. (ii) [Co(NH3)6]3+: NH3 is a strong field ligand, so it is low spin: t2g6 eg0. (c) In [NiCl4]2−, Cl− is a weak field ligand; Ni2+ (d8) remains in a high-spin arrangement (e4 t2^4) with 2 unpaired electrons, making it paramagnetic. In [Ni(CO)4], Ni is in the zero oxidation state (d10) and CO is a strong field ligand causing pairing; all electrons are paired (sp3, tetrahedral), making it diamagnetic.
keyPoints: eg orbitals (dz2, dx2−y2) raised in octahedral field (point toward ligands)
[CoF6]3−: high spin t2g4eg2; [Co(NH3)6]3+: low spin t2g6eg0
[NiCl4]2− (Ni2+, d8, weak field) paramagnetic; [Ni(CO)4] (Ni0, d10, all paired) diamagnetic

subject: Chemistry
text: An organic compound (X) has the molecular formula C5H10O. Draw structures for (X) if it: (I) does not give Tollen's test but gives a positive iodoform test. (II) does not give Tollen's test and iodoform test but undergoes Aldol condensation. (III) undergoes Cannizzaro's reaction. Also, show how each of the following compounds can be converted to benzoic acid: (I) Acetophenone (II) Ethyl benzene (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (I) Positive iodoform, no Tollens' test → a methyl ketone: pentan-2-one, CH3-CO-CH2-CH2-CH3. (II) No Tollens', no iodoform, but undergoes Aldol condensation → a ketone with alpha-hydrogens but no CH3-CO- group: pentan-3-one, CH3-CH2-CO-CH2-CH3. (III) Undergoes Cannizzaro's reaction → an aldehyde with no alpha-hydrogen: 2,2-dimethylpropanal, (CH3)3C-CHO. Conversion to benzoic acid: (I) Acetophenone (C6H5COCH3) is oxidised by the haloform reaction (NaOI/I2+NaOH, followed by acidification) which cleaves the methyl ketone to give benzoic acid + iodoform (CHI3). (II) Ethyl benzene is oxidised with hot alkaline KMnO4 (or acidified K2Cr2O7), which oxidises the side chain fully to -COOH regardless of chain length, followed by acidification, to give benzoic acid.
keyPoints: (I) pentan-2-one; (II) pentan-3-one; (III) 2,2-dimethylpropanal (pivaldehyde)
Acetophenone → haloform reaction (NaOI) → benzoic acid + CHI3
Ethyl benzene → hot alkaline KMnO4 oxidation → benzoic acid

text: (i) Draw structure of the 2,4-dinitrophenyl hydrazone derivative of benzaldehyde. (ii) Arrange the following in increasing order of their reactivity towards HCN: Di-tert. butyl ketone, Acetaldehyde, Acetone. (iii) Give a simple chemical test to distinguish between benzoic acid and ethyl benzoate. (iv) Write the name of the reagent to convert Ethanenitrile to Ethanal. (2026 Board)

text: From the given data of E° values, answer the following questions: E°(M2+/M) in V: V=−1.18, Cr=−0.91, Mn=−1.18, Fe=−0.44, Co=−0.28, Ni=−0.25, Cu=+0.34. (I) Why does E°(M2+/M) show irregular trend in the above values? (II) Why is E°(Cu2+/Cu) value exceptionally positive? (III) Why is E°(Mn2+/Mn) value highly negative? Also write the ionic equations for the oxidising action of potassium permanganate for its reaction with I− in both acidic and alkaline solutions. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (I) E°(M2+/M) depends on the sum of enthalpy of sublimation, ionisation enthalpy and hydration enthalpy of M2+, none of which vary regularly across the 3d series, so the net E° values also show an irregular trend. (II) Cu has a high enthalpy of atomisation (sublimation) and a low hydration enthalpy of Cu2+, so the overall energy required to convert Cu(s) to Cu2+(aq) is not compensated, making the process unfavourable — Cu2+/Cu has an unusually positive (least negative) reduction potential, i.e. Cu does not easily get oxidised/liberate H2 from acids. (III) Mn2+ has an extra-stable exactly half-filled 3d5 configuration; the high stability of Mn2+ favours the oxidation Mn → Mn2+, making E°(Mn2+/Mn) highly negative. Ionic equations for MnO4− + I−: In acidic medium: 2MnO4− + 16H+ + 10I− → 2Mn2+ + 8H2O + 5I2. In alkaline/neutral medium: 2MnO4− + H2O + I− → 2MnO2 + 2OH− + IO3−.
keyPoints: Irregular E° trend: sum of sublimation, ionisation and hydration enthalpies varies non-uniformly
Cu2+/Cu positive: high atomisation enthalpy + low hydration enthalpy of Cu2+
Mn2+/Mn very negative: extra stability of half-filled d5 Mn2+ favours oxidation
Acidic: 2MnO4−+16H++10I−→2Mn2++8H2O+5I2; Alkaline: 2MnO4−+H2O+I−→2MnO2+2OH−+IO3−

subject: Chemistry
text: (i) Name a member of the lanthanoid series which exhibits +4 oxidation state, and which exhibits +2 oxidation state. (ii) Why do transition metals act as good catalysts? (iii) Why does Cr have higher melting point than Mn? (iv) What happens when acidic solution of potassium permanganate is allowed to stand for sometime? Give the equation involved. What is this type of reaction called? (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (i) Cerium (Ce) commonly exhibits the +4 oxidation state (Ce4+); Europium (Eu) commonly exhibits the +2 oxidation state (Eu2+). (ii) Transition metals act as good catalysts because of their variable oxidation states, which allow them to form intermediate complexes and provide a lower activation energy alternative pathway for reactions; they also have large surface area (in finely divided/adsorbed form) to adsorb reactants and their unpaired d-electrons help form bonds with reactant molecules. (iii) Cr (3d5 4s1) has more unpaired electrons available for stronger metallic/covalent interatomic bonding than Mn (3d5 4s2), which has an exceptionally stable half-filled d5 configuration that resists pairing/bonding, giving Mn weaker interatomic bonds and a lower melting point than Cr. (iv) Acidic KMnO4 solution slowly decomposes on standing, releasing oxygen and forming brown MnO2: 4MnO4− + 4H+ → 4MnO2 + 3O2 + 2H2O. This is a type of auto-oxidation-reduction (disproportionation) reaction.
keyPoints: Ce shows +4 (Ce4+); Eu shows +2 (Eu2+)
Catalytic activity: variable oxidation states + large surface area + intermediate complex formation
Cr > Mn m.p.: Cr has more unpaired e− for stronger bonding (Mn's d5 4s2 resists bonding)
4MnO4−+4H+→4MnO2+3O2+2H2O — disproportionation (auto-redox) reaction

subject: Chemistry
text: What type of deviation from Raoult's law is shown by mixture of ethanol and acetone? Give reason. What will happen to the boiling point of the solution on mixing ethanol and acetone? (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: Ethanol and acetone show positive deviation from Raoult's law. In pure ethanol, molecules are held by strong hydrogen bonding; when acetone is added, it disrupts this H-bonding without forming equally strong new interactions, so the A-B interactions are weaker than A-A and B-B interactions. This increases the escaping tendency of molecules, so the vapour pressure of the mixture is higher than that predicted by Raoult's law, and the boiling point of the solution decreases (is lower than that of the pure components).
keyPoints: Positive deviation from Raoult's law
Ethanol's H-bonding is disrupted by acetone; weaker A-B interactions
Higher vapour pressure → lower boiling point of the mixture

subject: Chemistry
text: Differentiate between the following: (i) Acidic amino acids and basic amino acids (ii) Nucleotide and Nucleoside (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (i) Acidic amino acids contain an extra -COOH group in the side chain (more carboxylic groups than amino groups), e.g. aspartic acid, glutamic acid, and their solutions are acidic. Basic amino acids contain an extra -NH2 (or basic) group in the side chain (more amino groups than carboxylic groups), e.g. lysine, arginine, and their solutions are basic. text: What type of deviation is shown by a mixture of chloroform and acetone from Raoult's law? Give reason. What will happen to the boiling point of the solution on mixing chloroform and acetone? (2026 Board)

keyPoints: Fibrous protein: parallel chains, insoluble (e.g. keratin); Globular: coiled/spherical, soluble (e.g. insulin)

text: (B)(a) Write the reagents which are used in the given conversions: (i) Phenol to 2,4,6-tribromophenol (ii) Propene to propan-1-ol (iii) Butan-2-one to butan-2-ol (b) Explain the mechanism of acid catalyzed hydration of alkene to form corresponding alcohol. (2026 Board)
modelAnswer: (a)(i) Reagent: Br2 water (excess, at room temperature) — phenol's strongly activated ring undergoes electrophilic substitution at all available o,p positions to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol directly, no catalyst needed. (ii) Reagent: B2H6 (diborane) followed by H2O2/NaOH — hydroboration-oxidation gives anti-Markovnikov addition of water, converting propene to propan-1-ol. (iii) Reagent: NaBH4 or LiAlH4 — reduces the ketone to the corresponding secondary alcohol, butan-2-ol. (b) Mechanism of acid-catalysed hydration: Step 1: The alkene's pi electrons attack a proton from the acid catalyst (H3O+), forming the more stable carbocation (Markovnikov addition, e.g. secondary/tertiary carbocation preferred). Step 2: A water molecule (nucleophile) attacks the electrophilic carbocation, forming a protonated alcohol (oxonium ion). Step 3: Loss of a proton from the oxonium ion (deprotonation by another water molecule) regenerates the acid catalyst and gives the final alcohol.
keyPoints: Phenol → tribromophenol: Br2 water (no catalyst needed)

text: Define molar conductivity (Λm). How does it vary with concentration for strong electrolytes?
modelAnswer: Molar conductivity (Λm) is defined as the conducting power of all the ions produced by one mole of an electrolyte, placed between two electrodes 1 cm apart. Λm = κ/c, where κ is conductivity and c is molar concentration. For strong electrolytes, Λm increases gradually on dilution (concentration decreases) because inter-ionic attractions decrease, following Kohlrausch's law: Λm = Λ°m − A√c.
keyPoints: Λm = κ/c (SI: S m² mol⁻¹)
For strong electrolytes: Λm increases on dilution

subject: Chemistry
text: Explain the following: (i) Why is the C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene shorter than in chloroalkanes? (ii) Why do aryl halides undergo electrophilic substitution and not nucleophilic substitution?
modelAnswer:
(i) In chlorobenzene, the lone pairs on Cl are delocalised into the benzene ring (resonance), giving the C–Cl bond partial double bond character. This makes the bond shorter and stronger than in chloroalkanes where no such resonance occurs.
(ii) Aryl halides have high electron density at the ring due to delocalization. Electrophiles attack easily. Nucleophilic substitution is difficult because the ring π electrons repel nucleophiles, and the sp² carbon is less susceptible to nucleophilic attack.
keyPoints: C–Cl shorter in chlorobenzene due to resonance/partial double bond character
Resonance donates electrons from Cl into ring
Electrophilic substitution: benzene ring is electron-rich
Nucleophilic substitution blocked by electron density and sp² geometry

subject: Chemistry
text: What are enzymes? Explain the lock and key model of enzyme action.
modelAnswer:
Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly proteins, that speed up biochemical reactions without themselves being consumed. They are highly specific in their action.

Lock and key model (Emil Fischer): The enzyme has an 'active site' with a specific shape (lock) that exactly complements the shape of the substrate (key). The substrate fits precisely into the active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex. The reaction proceeds and products are released, restoring the enzyme. The specificity of enzymes is explained by the complementary shapes of active site and substrate.
keyPoints: Enzymes: protein catalysts, highly specific
Active site: specific region where substrate binds
Lock and key: substrate shape complements active site (Emil Fischer)
Enzyme-substrate complex formed → products released → enzyme regenerated

subject: Chemistry
text: Distinguish between molecularity and order of reaction.
modelAnswer:
Molecularity: The number of reacting species (atoms, ions, molecules) that collide simultaneously in an elementary reaction. It is always a positive integer (1, 2, or 3). It is a theoretical concept applicable only to elementary reactions.

Order of reaction: The sum of the powers of the concentration terms in the experimentally determined rate law (rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, order = m+n). It can be a fraction, zero, or integer. It is determined experimentally and applies to both elementary and complex reactions.
keyPoints: Molecularity: number of colliding species in elementary step, always integer
Order: sum of exponents in rate law, can be fraction/zero
Molecularity: theoretical; Order: experimental
Molecularity: only for elementary; Order: elementary and complex

subject: Chemistry
text: Using crystal field theory, explain the colour of [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ complex ion.
modelAnswer:
[Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ has Ti³⁺ with configuration 3d¹ (one electron in d-orbital). In the octahedral crystal field, the d-orbitals split into lower t₂g (3 orbitals) and higher eg (2 orbitals) sets with energy difference Δₒ.

The single d electron occupies the lower t₂g level in the ground state. When white light falls on the complex, the electron absorbs energy from the visible region (wavelength corresponding to green light, ~490–500 nm) and is promoted from t₂g to eg. The complementary colour to green is violet/purple, which is the colour observed. Hence [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ appears violet/purple.
keyPoints: Ti³⁺: 3d¹ configuration
Octahedral splitting: t₂g (lower) and eg (higher)
d-d transition: t₂g → eg absorbs visible light
Absorbs green (~490 nm), transmits/reflects violet-purple → appears violet

subject: Chemistry
text: A compound A (C₈H₉N) is a primary amine. On treating with CHCl₃/KOH it gives a foul-smelling compound B. A on diazotization followed by coupling with phenol gives an azo dye C. Identify A, B and C. Write the reaction for formation of C.
modelAnswer:
A is a primary amine with formula C₈H₉N. A primary amine can be p-methylbenzylamine (C₆H₄-CH₃-CH₂NH₂) or N,N-dimethylaniline (but that is tertiary).

Given: primary amine, gives carbylamine (CHCl₃/KOH) → B is an isocyanide (carbylamine test). Diazotisation and coupling with phenol → azo dye.

Likely A = p-toluidine (CH₃C₆H₄NH₂, MW = 107, C₇H₉N). If C₈H₉N: could be 4-ethylaniline (C₂H₅C₆H₄NH₂).

A (primary aromatic amine) → diazotization: A + NaNO₂/HCl/0–5°C → ArN₂⁺Cl⁻ → coupling with phenol in alkaline medium → Ar–N=N–C₆H₄OH (azo dye C, orange/red colour).
keyPoints: A: primary aromatic amine (C₈H₉N, e.g., 4-ethylaniline)
B: isocyanide (foul smell) — carbylamine test confirms primary amine
C: azo dye formed by diazonium coupling with phenol
Reaction: ArN₂⁺ + C₆H₅OH → Ar-N=N-C₆H₄OH + H⁺

subject: Chemistry
text: What is optical isomerism? Give one example of a chiral molecule. Draw the two enantiomers and explain their relationship.
modelAnswer:
Optical isomerism: A type of stereoisomerism in which compounds have the same molecular formula and connectivity but differ in the spatial arrangement of atoms, such that one molecule is the non-superimposable mirror image of the other. Such compounds are called enantiomers and the carbon bearing four different groups is called a chiral carbon.

Example: Lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid), CH₃CH(OH)COOH — the central C bears –CH₃, –OH, –COOH and –H, all four different groups.

The two enantiomers are D-(−)-lactic acid and L-(+)-lactic acid (mirror images). They have identical physical properties except for the direction of rotation of plane-polarised light (+/−). Their relationship: non-superimposable mirror images (enantiomers).
keyPoints: Chiral carbon: four different groups attached
Enantiomers: non-superimposable mirror images
Example: lactic acid CH₃CH(OH)COOH
Enantiomers differ only in optical rotation (+/−)

subject: Chemistry
text: Give two reactions that distinguish between aldehydes and ketones.
modelAnswer:
(i) Tollens' test (silver mirror test): Aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal AgNO₃) to give a silver mirror. Ketones do not react.
RCHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 2OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + 2Ag↓ + 4NH₃ + H₂O

(ii) Fehling's test: Aldehydes (aliphatic) reduce Fehling's solution to give brick-red Cu₂O precipitate. Ketones do not react.
RCHO + 2Cu²⁺ + 5OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + Cu₂O↓ + 3H₂O

Both tests are positive for aldehydes and negative for ketones.
keyPoints: Tollens' test: RCHO → silver mirror (Ag↓); ketones no reaction
Fehling's test: RCHO → brick-red Cu₂O; ketones no reaction
Both tests based on reducing property of aldehyde group

subject: Chemistry
text: Explain why aniline is a weaker base than cyclohexylamine.
modelAnswer:
In aniline (C₆H₅NH₂), the lone pair of nitrogen is delocalised into the benzene ring through resonance. This decreases the electron density on nitrogen, making it less available for protonation. Hence aniline is a weaker base.

In cyclohexylamine (C₆H₁₁NH₂), the lone pair on N is not delocalised (no aromatic ring). The nitrogen has higher electron density and is a better proton acceptor. Hence cyclohexylamine is a stronger base than aniline.
keyPoints: Aniline: lone pair delocalised into benzene ring (resonance) → reduced availability for H⁺
Cyclohexylamine: no resonance, lone pair fully available for protonation
Conclusion: aniline weaker base than cyclohexylamine

subject: Chemistry
text: Describe the preparation and properties of potassium dichromate (K₂Cr₂O₇). Give its action with H₂S and FeSO₄.
modelAnswer:
Preparation: Chrome iron ore (FeCr₂O₄) is fused with Na₂CO₃ in air to give sodium chromate (Na₂CrO₄). This is treated with H₂SO₄ to give sodium dichromate (Na₂Cr₂O₇), which on treatment with KCl gives K₂Cr₂O₇.

Properties: Orange crystalline solid. In acidic solution, Cr₂O₇²⁻ is a powerful oxidising agent (Cr is reduced from +6 to +3).

Action with H₂S: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3H₂S + 8H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3S + 7H₂O (H₂S oxidised to S)

Action with FeSO₄: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O (Fe²⁺ oxidised to Fe³⁺)
keyPoints: Prepared from chrome iron ore via Na₂CrO₄ → Na₂Cr₂O₇ → K₂Cr₂O₇
Orange solid, powerful oxidising agent in acid
With H₂S: oxidises S²⁻ to S, Cr⁶⁺ → Cr³⁺
With FeSO₄: oxidises Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺

subject: Chemistry
text: What is denaturation of proteins? How does it occur? Give an example.
modelAnswer:
Denaturation is the process by which the secondary and tertiary structure of a protein is disrupted without breaking peptide bonds (primary structure is intact). The protein loses its biological activity.

How it occurs: Physical methods (heat, ultraviolet radiation, mechanical agitation) or chemical agents (strong acids/bases, organic solvents like urea) break the weak interactions (H-bonds, hydrophobic interactions, disulfide bridges sometimes) that maintain the 3D structure.

Example: (i) Boiling of egg white — the albumin protein is denatured by heat, changing from soluble to insoluble coagulated form. (ii) Curdling of milk by acids — casein protein is denatured.
keyPoints: Denaturation: disruption of secondary/tertiary structure (primary intact)
Causes: heat, acids/bases, organic solvents, UV
Protein loses biological activity
Examples: boiling egg white, curdling milk

subject: Chemistry
text: What is van't Hoff factor (i)? A 0.1 m aqueous solution of a weak acid has a freezing point depression of 0.198°C. Calculate the degree of dissociation if Kf = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹.
modelAnswer:
Van't Hoff factor (i) = observed colligative property / calculated colligative property for no dissociation. For electrolytes that dissociate, i > 1; for those that associate, i < 1; for non-electrolytes, i = 1.

Given: ΔTf = 0.198°C, m = 0.1 mol/kg, Kf = 1.86
Calculated ΔTf (without dissociation) = Kf × m = 1.86 × 0.1 = 0.186°C
i = observed/calculated = 0.198/0.186 = 1.065

For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻: i = 1 + α (if α << 1)
1.065 = 1 + α
α = 0.065 = 6.5%
keyPoints: i = observed ΔTf / theoretical ΔTf = 0.198/0.186 = 1.065
For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻: i = 1 + α
α = i − 1 = 0.065 (6.5% degree of dissociation)

subject: Chemistry
text: Define specific conductivity (κ) and molar conductivity (Λm). What is the relationship between them?
modelAnswer:
Specific conductivity (κ): The conductance of a solution of unit length (1 cm) and unit cross-sectional area (1 cm²). Units: S cm⁻¹ or S m⁻¹.

Molar conductivity (Λm): The conducting power of all the ions produced by one mole of an electrolyte, in a solution of given concentration. Units: S cm² mol⁻¹ or S m² mol⁻¹.

Relationship: Λm = (κ × 1000) / M, where M is the molarity (mol L⁻¹).
Or in SI: Λm = κ / c, where c is in mol m⁻³.
keyPoints: κ: conductance per unit length and area; S cm⁻¹
Λm: conductance of all ions from 1 mol electrolyte; S cm² mol⁻¹
Relation: Λm = (κ × 1000)/M (when κ in S cm⁻¹, M in mol L⁻¹)

subject: Chemistry
text: Explain the effect of temperature on the rate of reaction using Arrhenius equation. What is the activation energy?
modelAnswer:
Arrhenius equation: k = Ae^(−Ea/RT)
where k = rate constant, A = frequency factor (pre-exponential factor), Ea = activation energy, R = gas constant (8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), T = temperature in Kelvin.

Effect of temperature: As T increases, e^(−Ea/RT) increases (exponent becomes less negative), so k increases exponentially. For most reactions, a 10°C rise approximately doubles the rate.

Activation energy (Ea): The minimum energy that reactant molecules must possess for a collision to be effective (result in a reaction). It is the energy difference between the transition state and the reactants.

Log form: log k = log A − Ea/(2.303RT). A plot of log k vs 1/T gives a straight line with slope = −Ea/(2.303R).
keyPoints: Arrhenius equation: k = Ae^(−Ea/RT)
Ea = activation energy (minimum energy for reaction)
As T increases, k increases exponentially
Slope of log k vs 1/T graph = −Ea/(2.303R)

subject: Chemistry
text: Explain the stability of coordination compounds with reference to chelate effect. Give one example.
modelAnswer:
Chelate effect: Chelate complexes (those formed by polydentate/chelating ligands) are thermodynamically more stable than analogous complexes with monodentate ligands. This extra stability is called the chelate effect.

Reason: When a chelating ligand replaces monodentate ligands, there is a net increase in entropy (ΔS > 0) because more free particles are produced. By ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, a positive ΔS makes ΔG more negative, increasing stability.

Also, the ring structure formed (chelate ring) restricts rotation and reduces the probability of both donor atoms leaving simultaneously.

Example: [Cu(en)₂]²⁺ (with two bidentate en ligands) is more stable than [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ (with four monodentate NH₃) even though the donor atoms are similar (N in both cases). This is the chelate effect.
keyPoints: Chelate effect: extra stability of complexes with polydentate ligands
Thermodynamic basis: replacement of monodentate by chelating ligand increases entropy
ΔG more negative due to +TΔS contribution
Example: [Cu(en)₂]²⁺ more stable than [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺

subject: Chemistry
text: Describe the SN1 and SN2 mechanisms of nucleophilic substitution. Which mechanism is followed by tertiary alkyl halides?
modelAnswer:
SN1 (Unimolecular Nucleophilic Substitution):
• Two-step mechanism: (1) slow ionisation → carbocation intermediate; (2) fast attack by nucleophile.
• Rate = k[RX] (first order, depends only on [substrate]).
• Favoured by: tertiary substrates (stable 3° carbocation), polar protic solvents.
• Gives racemisation (mixture of retention and inversion).

SN2 (Bimolecular Nucleophilic Substitution):
• One-step concerted mechanism: nucleophile attacks from the back while leaving group departs.
• Rate = k[RX][Nu] (second order).
• Favoured by: primary substrates, strong nucleophiles, polar aprotic solvents.
• Gives inversion of configuration (Walden inversion).

Tertiary alkyl halides follow SN1 because the 3° carbocation intermediate is stabilised by hyperconjugation and +I effect of three alkyl groups.
keyPoints: SN1: two-step, rate = k[RX], carbocation intermediate, racemisation
SN2: one-step concerted, rate = k[RX][Nu], inversion (Walden)
Tertiary halides: SN1 (stable 3° carbocation)
Primary halides: SN2 (less steric hindrance)

subject: Chemistry
text: Describe the structure of DNA. How does it differ from RNA?
modelAnswer:
DNA (Deoxyribonucleic acid):
• Double-stranded helix (Watson-Crick model).
• Sugar: 2'-deoxyribose.
• Bases: Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C), Thymine (T).
• Base pairing: A–T (2 H-bonds), G–C (3 H-bonds).
• Two strands are antiparallel and complementary.
• Found mainly in nucleus; carries genetic information.

Differences from RNA:
• RNA is usually single-stranded; DNA is double-stranded.
• RNA has ribose sugar; DNA has deoxyribose.
• RNA has Uracil (U) instead of Thymine (T).
• RNA is found in nucleus and cytoplasm; DNA mainly in nucleus.
• RNA has shorter lifespan; DNA is more stable.
keyPoints: DNA: double helix, deoxyribose, A-T and G-C base pairs
RNA: single-stranded, ribose, Uracil instead of Thymine
DNA: mainly nucleus, stable; RNA: nucleus + cytoplasm, less stable
Antiparallel strands in DNA held by H-bonds

subject: Chemistry
text: State and explain Henry's law. Give two applications.
modelAnswer:
Henry's law: At constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of the gas above the liquid.
p = KH × x, where p = partial pressure, x = mole fraction of gas in solution, KH = Henry's law constant.

Explanation: Higher pressure forces more gas molecules into solution (increases solubility). KH has units of pressure; a higher KH means lower solubility.

Applications:
(i) Carbonated beverages: CO₂ is dissolved in soft drinks under high pressure. When the bottle is opened, pressure drops and CO₂ escapes (fizzing).
(ii) Deep-sea diving: At high pressure underwater, N₂ dissolves in blood. If the diver surfaces too quickly, N₂ comes out of solution forming bubbles (the bends/decompression sickness).
keyPoints: Henry's law: p = KH × x (solubility ∝ partial pressure)
KH = Henry's law constant (higher KH → lower solubility)
Application 1: carbonated beverages (CO₂ under pressure)
Application 2: decompression sickness in divers (N₂ in blood)

subject: Chemistry
text: Explain the acidity of phenol. Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol but less acidic than carbonic acid?
modelAnswer:
Acidity of phenol: Phenol is acidic because it can donate a proton to form a stable phenoxide ion (C₆H₅O⁻).
C₆H₅OH ⇌ C₆H₅O⁻ + H⁺

The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance — the negative charge is delocalised over the benzene ring (ortho and para positions). This stabilisation makes phenol more acidic than alcohols.

Phenol vs Ethanol: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH → C₂H₅O⁻) — the ethoxide ion has no resonance stabilisation. Phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised. Hence phenol (pKa ≈ 10) is far more acidic than ethanol (pKa ≈ 16).

Phenol vs Carbonic acid: Carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) has two highly electronegative O atoms that stabilise the resulting HCO₃⁻ anion by induction in addition to resonance. The pKa of carbonic acid (≈6.3) is lower than phenol (≈10), so carbonic acid is stronger — hence CO₂ + H₂O reacts with sodium phenoxide to re-form phenol.
keyPoints: Phenol ionises to give resonance-stabilised phenoxide ion
Phenoxide ion: negative charge delocalised over ortho/para positions
Phenol (pKa 10) more acidic than ethanol (pKa 16) due to resonance
Phenol (pKa 10) less acidic than H₂CO₃ (pKa 6.3) due to inductive effect of two O atoms

subject: Chemistry
text: Explain the synthesis of azo dyes from primary aromatic amines. Give the reaction for preparation of p-hydroxyazobenzene.
modelAnswer:
Azo dyes are synthesised in two steps:

Step 1 — Diazotisation: A primary aromatic amine is treated with NaNO₂ and HCl at 0–5°C to form a diazonium salt.
C₆H₅NH₂ + NaNO₂ + 2HCl → C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + NaCl + 2H₂O

Step 2 — Coupling reaction: The diazonium salt reacts with an electron-rich aromatic compound (phenol or amine) in alkaline or mild acidic conditions.
C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + C₆H₅OH → C₆H₅–N=N–C₆H₄–OH (p-hydroxyazobenzene, orange dye) + HCl

Coupling occurs at the para position (activated by –OH group) to give an azo compound (R–N=N–R') characterised by the azo linkage (–N=N–). These compounds are intensely coloured and used as dyes.
keyPoints: Step 1: Diazotisation — ArNH₂ + NaNO₂/HCl/0-5°C → ArN₂⁺Cl⁻
Step 2: Coupling — ArN₂⁺ + phenol/amine → Ar-N=N-Ar' (azo dye)
Coupling at para position of activated ring
p-Hydroxyazobenzene: C₆H₅-N=N-C₆H₄-OH (orange colour)

subject: Chemistry
text: Define molecularity of a reaction. State any one condition in which a bimolecular reaction may be kinetically of first order. (2024 Board)
modelAnswer:
Molecularity is the number of reacting species (atoms, ions or molecules) that come together simultaneously to bring about a chemical change in an elementary reaction. For example, molecularity of A + B → P is 2 (bimolecular).

A bimolecular reaction appears to be of first order (pseudo-first order) when one of the reactants is present in large excess (e.g., in aqueous solutions where water is a reactant, or when one reactant is in very high concentration compared to the other). Its concentration remains essentially constant throughout the reaction, so the rate depends only on the concentration of the other reactant.
keyPoints: Molecularity = number of species colliding in a single elementary step
Pseudo-first order: one reactant in large excess keeps its concentration effectively constant
Example: acid hydrolysis of ester in excess water, rate = k[ester]

subject: Chemistry
text: What happens when D-glucose is treated with the following reagents? (a) HI (b) Conc. HNO3 (2024 Board)
modelAnswer:
(a) D-glucose + HI → n-hexane. HI reduces glucose by replacing all –OH groups (except the terminal –CHO and –CH2OH which are reduced) with –H, ultimately giving n-hexane (a straight-chain 6-carbon alkane). This confirms the carbon skeleton is unbranched.
(b) D-glucose + conc. HNO3 → glucaric acid (saccharic acid). The terminal aldehyde (–CHO) and the primary alcohol (–CH2OH) are both oxidised to –COOH groups, giving a dicarboxylic acid (glucaric acid). This confirms glucose has a straight chain with a –CHO at one end and –CH2OH at the other.
keyPoints: (a) HI reduces glucose to n-hexane (all hydroxyls removed), confirming unbranched 6-C chain
(b) Conc. HNO3 oxidises both ends (−CHO and −CH2OH) to −COOH, giving glucaric/saccharic acid
Both reactions confirm the linear structure of glucose

subject: Chemistry
text: Give reasons for the following: (i) Grignard reagent should be prepared under anhydrous conditions. (ii) Alkyl halides give alcohol with aqueous KOH whereas alkenes are formed in the presence of alcoholic KOH. (2024 Board)
modelAnswer:
(i) Grignard reagents (RMgX) are extremely reactive towards water. Even traces of moisture cause the Grignard reagent to react with water (hydrolysis: RMgX + H2O → RH + Mg(OH)X), decomposing it before it can be used. Therefore, anhydrous conditions (dry ether solvent, dry apparatus) are essential.

(ii) In aqueous KOH, OH⁻ is a good nucleophile and the reaction proceeds by SN2 substitution: R–X + OH⁻ → R–OH + X⁻. In alcoholic KOH, OH⁻ acts as a strong base (less solvated, more basic character) and removes a β-hydrogen in an E2 elimination reaction: R–CH2–CH2X + OH⁻ → R–CH=CH2 + H2O + X⁻.
keyPoints: (i) Grignard reagent decomposes with water (RMgX + H2O → RH + Mg(OH)X); anhydrous conditions prevent this
(ii) Aqueous KOH: OH⁻ acts as nucleophile → SN2 substitution → alcohol
(ii) Alcoholic KOH: OH⁻ acts as base → E2 elimination → alkene

subject: Chemistry
text: Write the chemical equation when: (a) Butan-2-one is treated with Zn(Hg) and conc. HCl. (b) Two molecules of benzaldehyde are treated with conc. NaOH. (2024 Board)
modelAnswer:
(a) Clemmensen reduction of butan-2-one:
CH3–CO–CH2–CH3 + Zn(Hg)/conc. HCl → CH3–CH2–CH2–CH3 (butane)
The C=O group is reduced to –CH2–.

(b) Cannizzaro reaction of benzaldehyde:
2C6H5–CHO + NaOH (conc.) → C6H5–COONa + C6H5–CH2OH
(sodium benzoate + benzyl alcohol)
One molecule is oxidised to carboxylate and the other is reduced to alcohol.
keyPoints: (a) Clemmensen reduction: C=O → CH2 using Zn(Hg)/HCl; butan-2-one → butane
(b) Cannizzaro reaction (aldehydes without α-H): one is oxidised → carboxylate, other reduced → alcohol
Products: sodium benzoate + benzyl alcohol

subject: Chemistry
text: When a certain conductivity cell was filled with 0.05 M KCl solution, it has a resistance of 100 ohm at 25°C. When the same cell was filled with 0.02 M AgNO3 solution, the resistance was 90 ohm. Calculate the conductivity and molar conductivity of AgNO3 solution. (Given: Conductivity of 0.05 M KCl solution = 1.35 × 10⁻² ohm⁻¹cm⁻¹) (2024 Board)
modelAnswer:
Step 1: Find cell constant.
Cell constant = conductivity × resistance = 1.35×10⁻² × 100 = 1.35 cm⁻¹

Step 2: Conductivity of AgNO3.
κ(AgNO3) = cell constant / R(AgNO3) = 1.35 / 90 = 1.5×10⁻² ohm⁻¹cm⁻¹

subject: Chemistry
text: (a) Which of the following is an allylic halide? (i) CH3–CH=CH–Br (ii) CH2=CH–CH(Br)–CH3. (b) Out of chlorobenzene and 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene, which is more reactive towards nucleophilic substitution and why? (c) Which isomer of C4H9Cl has the lowest boiling point? (2024 Board)
modelAnswer:
(a) (ii) CH2=CH–CH(Br)–CH3 is an allylic halide because the Br is attached to a carbon adjacent (allylic position) to the C=C double bond.
(Note: (i) CH3–CH=CH–Br is a vinylic halide because Br is directly on the sp2 carbon of the double bond.)

(b) 2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene is far more reactive towards nucleophilic substitution. The three electron-withdrawing nitro groups at ortho and para positions strongly decrease the electron density on the ring, particularly on the carbon bearing the Cl. This activates the ring towards nucleophilic attack (SNAr mechanism) by stabilising the Meisenheimer complex (negative intermediate).

(c) Neopentyl chloride (2-chloro-2-methylpropane, i.e., (CH3)3C–CH2Cl) — wait, the correct answer is 2-chloro-2-methylpropane [(CH3)3CCl] (tert-butyl chloride), which has the lowest boiling point among C4H9Cl isomers because it is the most branched, reducing the surface area and hence van der Waals forces.
keyPoints: (a) (ii) is allylic halide; (i) is vinylic halide
(b) 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene is more reactive: three NO2 groups stabilise the Meisenheimer complex via electron withdrawal
(c) tert-butyl chloride [(CH3)3CCl] has the lowest boiling point due to highest branching

subject: Chemistry
text: Answer any three of the following: (a) What is peptide linkage? (b) What type of bonds hold a DNA double helix together? (c) Which one of the following is a polysaccharide? Sucrose, Glucose, Starch, Fructose. (d) Give one example each for water-soluble vitamins and fat-soluble vitamins. (2024 Board)
modelAnswer:
(a) A peptide linkage (peptide bond) is an amide bond (–CO–NH–) formed between the –COOH group of one amino acid and the –NH2 group of another, with elimination of water.

(b) Hydrogen bonds hold the two strands of the DNA double helix together. Specifically, complementary base pairs are connected by hydrogen bonds: A–T (2 H-bonds) and G–C (3 H-bonds).

(c) Starch is a polysaccharide. Sucrose is a disaccharide; glucose and fructose are monosaccharides.

(d) Water-soluble: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) or Vitamin B complex (e.g., B1 thiamine).
Fat-soluble: Vitamin A (retinol) or Vitamin D, E, or K.
keyPoints: Peptide linkage: amide bond (–CO–NH–) between –COOH and –NH2 with loss of water
DNA double helix held by hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs (A-T: 2, G-C: 3)
Polysaccharide: Starch (not sucrose=disaccharide, not glucose/fructose=monosaccharides)
Water-soluble: Vit C or B-group; Fat-soluble: Vit A, D, E or K
